\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

\subsection{Conclusions and Contributions}
\label{sec:contributions}

We have formalized injection detection on discrete activity events with a lifecycle. On the theoretical side, we have shown in a numbered proposition (Proposition~\ref{prop:ta}) that the detector family which thresholds only the predicted probability of labels adds nothing beyond the feasibility mask for label-consistent injections under a zero-false-alarm constraint, and we have derived the critical relative advance $\rho^*(\alpha,\sigma)$.

On the methodological side, we build a hard-constraint layer from the reference-model feasibility mask (zero violations on the cleaned normal data) and a timing channel from distributional sojourn times grouped by (device, operation); the two statistical channels are calibrated by conformal prediction and accumulated by {CUSUM} tests. Compared with decomposed timed automata and within-stage dependency models, our method differs in two respects: distributional durations allow early reports inside the guard to be accumulated, and feasibility comes from the reference model rather than being learned from logs.

The experiments show that physically infeasible injection is covered by the feasibility mask (net detection $0.95$); on gradual drift our method achieves $0.87$, while the label-only ablation scores zero; on early-completion replay at a $20\%$ injection rate it achieves $0.18$, higher than {BUTLA} and not significantly different from the {TABOR}-style baseline; and the mixture power curve predicted by the critical-relative-advance model agrees with the measurements. These results indicate that, for lifecycle activity events in industry, reference-model feasibility and distributional sojourn times are two kinds of evidence missing from label-only detection; the disadvantage on {A4}/{A6} shows that they cannot replace workflow structure.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\textbf{(1) State mimicry and message suppression lack a dedicated detection path.}
On {A4}/{A6} our detection is below that of the label-only ablation. There are two possible causes whose effects have not been separated: after the three-way split the structural channel receives only $\alpha/3$, and its state is the operation name, which is insensitive to the device. This limitation qualifies the comparison of ``six-class means'' but does not affect the claims about {A2} and {A3}/{A5}.

\textbf{(2) Without workpiece identities, material-flow invariants cannot serve as reliable constraints.}
The benign violation rate $q$ rises from $0.0054$ on the training fold to $0.047$ on the deployment stream, which caps single-message detection at only $0.21$ for $\alpha=0.01$. Approximate cross-case workpiece identities lower $q$ to $2.3\%$, still above $\alpha$, and end-to-end performance is the same as without the constraint, so the token constraint is not included in the detector. This limitation does not affect the three claims of this paper; it only means that the hard-constraint layer cannot yet cover cross-device material-flow forgery.

\textbf{(3) The main evaluation uses a single public log, synthetic injections, and reimplemented baselines.}
The main evaluation has only one public log that provides both {BPMN} and the activity lifecycle; attacks are synthesized by a reproducible injector; the baselines are reimplemented from the structural constraints of the original papers rather than taken from official code; and no comparison is made with learned sequence models that use time features. The workflow splits within the log, the official error-containing version, and the unseen workflows serve only as stress tests and cannot substitute for a second external dataset; under a temporal split the conformal guarantee no longer holds automatically, and duration kernels cannot be transferred across scenarios directly (Section~\ref{sec:boundary}). This limitation threatens the external validity of the results on {A2} and {A3}/{A5}, but does not affect Proposition~\ref{prop:ta}.

\subsection{Future Work}
\label{sec:future_work}

\textbf{(1) Validate material-token constraints on production lines with workpiece identifiers.}
This addresses Limitation~(2). With workpiece identities, if the benign violation rate in deployment can be brought down to the order of $\alpha$, token conservation could complement the hard-constraint layer and detect cross-device material-flow forgery.

\textbf{(2) Design a rule for allocating the false-alarm budget across channels without attack labels.}
This addresses Limitation~(1). The current $\alpha/3$ is the even Bonferroni split under a parallel OR decision, and the disadvantage on {A4}/{A6} may be related to the structural channel receiving only $\alpha/3$. An allocation rule must not use attack labels to tune thresholds in reverse.

\textbf{(3) Add a second external dataset, official baseline implementations, and learned sequence baselines.}
This addresses Limitation~(3). Testing the external validity of the conclusions requires another public log that provides both {BPMN} and the activity lifecycle, or official baseline implementations that accept this log format, complemented by learned sequence models with time features as competitors.

\textbf{(4) Study online recalibration of the duration kernel.}
This addresses Limitation~(3) and Section~\ref{sec:boundary}. The self-built scenarios show that transferring the duration kernel across scenarios sharply lowers {A3} detection or raises false alarms, whereas the feasibility mask need not be re-estimated. Future work could update the duration kernel adaptively per product type under gate protection, so that the detector need not be refitted from scratch after a product changeover.

\section{Data Availability}
\label{sec:data}

The {Fischertechnik} {Trier} smart-factory event log is released by its original authors~\cite{malburg2022trier}; a copy of the data is available on {Figshare} at \texttt{10.6084/m9.figshare.20130794}. The injection protocol, baseline reimplementations, diagnostic scripts, and evaluation archives are in the accompanying code repository, available from the corresponding author during review and to be made public upon acceptance. The main tables and box plots are read from JSON archives, and no quantile is filled in by hand. Paper-level {CSV} files are aggregated from the archives by \texttt{py -m tools.export\_experiments}. The self-built scenarios~I/II/III (configurations {A}/{B}/{C} in the code) are regenerated from seeds by \texttt{algorithm/plant.py}. {HAI} is used only to check the data dictionary and is not imported into the {CSV} files.

\begin{acks}
We thank the {University of Trier} for releasing an {IoT} event log with a {BPMN} reference model, which made it possible for the feasibility mask to come from an external reference model rather than being learned from the log.
\end{acks}
